c1.q: Is the thermostat fan set to ON or AUTO?
c1.help: Look for a fan switch or menu on the thermostat.

steps: With the fan on ON, the blower runs nonstop, including between heating cycles, so you feel room-temperature air.
Switch the fan to AUTO. The blower will then run only while the burners are heating.
If the air is still cold during a heating cycle, run the troubleshooter again with the fan on AUTO.

c2.q: When was the air filter last changed?
c2.help: The filter slides into a slot near the blower or in a return-air grille.
c: Over 3 months ago, or it looks grey

steps: Turn the furnace off at the thermostat.
Slide out the old filter and note the size printed on its edge (for example 16x25x1).
Insert the new filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the furnace.
Turn the heat back on. A clogged filter makes the furnace overheat, and a safety switch then shuts off the burners while the blower keeps pushing unheated air.

c3.q: Watch the burners through the viewing window. What happens when heat is called?
c3.help: Most furnaces have a small window or gap in the front panel.
c: Flame lights, then goes out within a few seconds
Flame stays lit, air is still cold

steps: Turn off power to the furnace at its service switch and shut the gas valve.
Remove the burner panel. The flame sensor is a thin metal rod in front of the burners, held by one screw.
Remove it and gently rub the rod with fine steel wool or a fine abrasive pad until it shines. Do not use sandpaper.
Reinstall it, restore gas and power, and test. If it keeps happening, the sensor or its wiring needs replacing.

c4.q: Is the furnace's status light blinking a code?
c4.help: Look through the small window on the lower blower panel for a red or green LED.
c: Yes, it is blinking a pattern

c_code.h: Read the error code, then decide
steps: Count the blinks and match them to the code chart on the inside of the furnace door.
Codes for pressure switch, ignition lockout or limit switch faults usually point to a blocked vent, a clogged condensate drain or a failed part.
Clear any snow or debris from outside vent pipes. If the code returns, call a technician and tell them the code.

c_duct.h: Possible duct or heat exchanger problem
steps: If the burners stay lit but the air stays cold, heat may not be reaching the vents. Check for disconnected ducts in an unfinished basement or attic.
Weak heat with the flame running can also mean a cracked heat exchanger, which can leak carbon monoxide.
Make sure your CO detector works and have a technician inspect the furnace.
No flame and no error code usually means a failed igniter, gas valve or control board.
Check that the gas valve next to the furnace is turned on (handle parallel to the pipe).
If it is on, schedule a technician. These parts involve gas and high voltage.

o1.q: Is the thermostat set to HEAT and above room temperature, with a working display?
o1.help: A blank display usually means dead batteries.
c: It was set to OFF or COOL

steps: Pull the thermostat off its wall plate or open the battery door.
Replace the batteries (usually AA or AAA).
Set it to HEAT, a few degrees above room temperature, and wait five minutes.
Switch the mode to HEAT.
Set the temperature at least 3 degrees above the current room temperature.
Some thermostats wait up to five minutes before starting the furnace to protect the equipment.

o2.q: Check the furnace power switch (it looks like a light switch on or near the furnace) and the breaker.
o2.help: People often switch it off by mistake, thinking it's a light.
c: The switch or breaker was off

steps: Turn the furnace switch on, or reset the breaker in your electrical panel.
If the breaker trips again right away, leave it off and call a technician. That points to an electrical fault.

o3.q: Is the front blower panel fully closed?
o3.help: Furnaces have a safety switch that cuts power when the lower door is not seated.

steps: Line up the panel and press it firmly until it clicks into place. This pushes the door safety switch closed.
Wait a minute for the furnace to restart its sequence.

o4.q: Is the status light on the control board blinking?
o4.help: Look through the small window on the lower panel.

steps: Count the blinks and find the code on the chart inside the furnace door.
A high-efficiency furnace often shuts down when the condensate drain clogs. Check that the drain line is not blocked.
For ignition, pressure switch or limit codes that keep coming back, call a technician with the code.
With power on and no light on the control board, the transformer, a fuse on the board or the board itself may have failed.
This involves 120-volt wiring. Schedule a technician.

l1.q: Is it leaking while the air conditioning runs, or while the heat runs?
l1.help: Your AC coil usually sits on top of the furnace.

steps: The cooling coil above the furnace drips water into a pan and out through a drain line. A clog makes the pan overflow onto the furnace.
Turn off the system. Find the PVC drain line and its cleanout cap.
Pour a cup of distilled vinegar into the cleanout, or use a wet/dry vacuum on the outside end of the line to pull the clog out.
If the drain pan itself is cracked or rusted through, call a technician.

l2.q: Does your furnace have white plastic (PVC) vent pipes?
l2.help: PVC pipes mean a high-efficiency condensing furnace. Metal pipes mean a standard-efficiency furnace.

l_cond.h: Check the condensate trap and pump
steps: High-efficiency furnaces make water as they run, and it drains through a trap and hose, sometimes into a small pump.
Turn off power. Look for a disconnected, cracked or clogged hose and reconnect or flush it.
If you have a condensate pump, check that its float moves freely and the pump runs when you lift the float. Pumps cost $50–80 to replace.
If the water is coming from a joint in the vent pipe, call a technician.
A standard furnace with a metal flue should not produce water. Leaking can mean exhaust is condensing in a poorly vented flue.
Poor venting can push carbon monoxide into your home.
Check that your CO detectors work, and schedule an inspection.

n1.q: What does the noise sound like?
n1.help: Listen right after the furnace starts and while it runs.
c: A loud bang or boom when it starts

n_bang.h: Turn the furnace off and call a technician
steps: A boom at startup usually means delayed ignition. Gas builds up before it lights, often because the burners are dirty.
Repeated delayed ignition can crack the heat exchanger.
Turn the furnace off at the thermostat and have the burners serviced before using it again.
Older furnaces use a belt that can slip or wear out. Newer direct-drive blowers squeal when motor bearings fail.
Turn off power and look at the blower. A cracked or loose belt can be replaced for a few dollars.
A failing motor needs a technician.
Turn off power and check that every access panel is seated and its screws are tight.
Look at ductwork connections near the furnace for loose sheet-metal screws.
If the rattle comes from inside the blower compartment, call a technician.
Metal on metal usually means the blower wheel has come loose or broken and is hitting its housing.
Running it can destroy the motor. Turn the furnace off and call a technician.
Whistling usually means the furnace is starving for air.
Replace the filter, and make sure the filter slot cover is in place.
Open closed supply vents and clear furniture off return-air grilles.
